paragraphs: Learning a causal graph involves determining which way its connections point. Observations can leave some directions unresolved, while experiments can provide additional information. This paper studies how to choose experiments when only a limited number are available. Its setting permits at most k experiments, each targeting one variable, with all targets chosen before experimental results arrive.

The authors formulate target selection as an optimization problem: maximize the average number of edge directions that the experiments resolve. They prove that this objective is submodular, meaning that additional targets have diminishing returns. This structure supports a greedy selection algorithm with a guarantee of at least a 1 − 1/e fraction of the optimal objective value.

They also introduce an accelerated version that can produce orders-of-magnitude speedups. On synthetic and real graphs, their approach resolves most edge directions with relatively few interventions compared with using observations alone. The contribution connects a restricted experimental budget to both a principled selection rule and a quantified approximation guarantee.
icml-2018-budgeted-experiment-design-for.tldr: A greedy experiment-selection method has a provable approximation guarantee and resolves most causal edge directions with few interventions in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Classification becomes computationally demanding when a model must consider a very large number of possible labels. Candidates vs. Noises Estimation, or CANE, divides this work between a small set of selected candidate classes and samples drawn from the remaining classes. The method uses this combination to estimate a classifier without the standard cost of processing every class.

The authors establish consistency and computational efficiency for the estimator. They also identify a condition for especially favorable statistical behavior: when the observed label falls among the selected candidates with high probability, the estimator's variance approaches that of maximum likelihood estimation. This makes the quality of candidate selection relevant to statistical precision as well as computation.

For practical selection, classes occupy the leaves of a tree searched with beam search. The authors also apply CANE to estimating word probabilities in neural language models. Their experiments report better prediction accuracy than Noise-Contrastive Estimation, its variants, and several leading tree classifiers, together with substantial speedups over methods whose cost grows linearly with the number of classes.
icml-2018-candidates-vs-noises-estimatio.tldr: CANE combines selected candidate labels with sampled alternatives to make large-class classification efficient while retaining strong statistical properties.

paragraphs: An optimization problem can have many equally good global solutions, leaving a further question: which one does a particular training method select? This paper studies that selection behavior, called implicit bias, for underdetermined linear models and separable linear classification problems. The focus is on the preference introduced by the optimization procedure itself.

The methods considered include Mirror Descent, Natural Gradient Descent, and Steepest Descent under different potentials and norms. These choices describe the geometry used by an optimizer to determine its updates. The authors investigate whether this geometry provides a way to characterize the solution that optimization ultimately reaches among the available possibilities.

A central part of the question is whether such a characterization can be independent of hyperparameters such as step size and momentum. That distinction matters because it separates a method's geometric preference from effects of its particular settings. The abstract presents the scope and research question rather than announcing a general answer, so the contribution described here is an investigation of when optimization geometry can explain solution selection.
icml-2018-characterizing-implicit-bias-i.tldr: The paper investigates whether optimization geometry characterizes the solutions selected in linear learning problems independently of hyperparameters.

paragraphs: This paper considers prediction when data items belong to a metric space but their representations and numerical distances are unavailable. The learner can instead choose three items and ask whether the first is closer to the second or the third. Such answers provide relative similarity information without exposing coordinates or exact distance values.

The authors construct a random forest for classification and regression using only these triplet comparisons. This extends the forest approach to a restricted information setting: the available evidence consists of chosen comparison queries rather than directly accessible features. Their theoretical analysis establishes sufficient conditions for consistency, giving circumstances under which learning from this information has a sound statistical basis.

Experiments assess both classification and regression and find the proposed forest efficient. It is also competitive with methods that receive the data's metric representation directly. The result suggests that relative comparisons can retain substantial predictive value in the evaluated settings, even when richer numerical descriptions are inaccessible. The consistency claim remains tied to the sufficient conditions established in the analysis.
icml-2018-comparison-based-random-forest.tldr: A random forest learns classification and regression from relative-distance comparisons alone, with conditional consistency guarantees and competitive experimental performance.

paragraphs: Interactions between sets of objects can be represented as matrices or tensors, such as users rating movies or proteins binding drugs. Reordering the objects changes their positions in this representation without changing the interactions themselves. This paper builds deep models around that symmetry: predictions should follow the same reordering rather than depend on arbitrary row or column positions.

The authors introduce a parameter-sharing scheme and prove it is maximally expressive under the permutation-equivariance constraint. Its parameter count does not depend on the number of objects, supporting use with large collections. The models can also answer queries about objects absent during training when interactions involving those objects have subsequently been observed.

Experiments show performance competitive with leading methods on matrix completion benchmarks. The authors also report strong generalization when extending predictions to new objects, both within the training domain and across domains, including transfer from movie ratings to music ratings. These findings connect a structural symmetry to practical scalability and reuse, while the new-object capability still relies on having observed interactions for those objects.
icml-2018-deep-models-of-interactions-ac.tldr: Permutation-equivariant interaction models combine expressive parameter sharing with competitive matrix completion and promising generalization to new objects and domains.

paragraphs: Training to minimize average error gives smaller groups less influence over the objective. If those groups receive worse predictions and consequently stop using a service, their influence can shrink further during subsequent training. This paper studies that feedback loop and shows how repeated empirical risk minimization can amplify representation disparity, including making an initially fair model unfair.

The proposed response is distributionally robust optimization. Instead of considering only the empirical distribution, it minimizes the worst risk among distributions close to it. This changes which errors drive learning without requiring the algorithm to know users' group identities. The authors prove that their approach controls minority-group risk at each time step in the setting they analyze.

The paper demonstrates examples where this method prevents disparity amplification while ordinary empirical risk minimization fails. It also reports improved minority-group user satisfaction in a real text autocomplete task. The findings make retention part of the fairness problem: a model's errors can reshape the population that supplies its future training data.
icml-2018-fairness-without-demographics-.tldr: Distributionally robust training can counter feedback loops that worsen minority-group performance without requiring demographic group identities.

paragraphs: Some learning problems make explicit gradient calculations too costly or unavailable. Zeroth-order methods address this by estimating a gradient from function evaluations. This paper focuses on asynchronous parallel versions for shared-memory machines, where the aim is to combine derivative-free optimization with parallel computation for large learning problems.

The authors examine why the earlier AsySZO algorithm has a convergence rate of O(1/√T) for smooth, potentially nonconvex problems. They then propose AsySZO+, with a theoretical rate of O(1/(bT)), where b is the mini-batch size. This improves the stated dependence on the iteration count and explicitly incorporates the contribution of mini-batching into the bound.

Experiments on ensemble learning support the theoretical motivation: AsySZO+ converges faster than the existing asynchronous and other stochastic zeroth-order algorithms considered. The significance is that avoiding explicit derivatives need not entail the slower rate of the earlier method in the analyzed setting. The claimed improvement concerns convergence behavior, with the experimental evidence supplied by the ensemble-learning application.
icml-2018-faster-derivative-free-stochas.tldr: AsySZO+ improves the analyzed convergence rate of asynchronous derivative-free optimization and converges faster in ensemble-learning experiments.

paragraphs: Minimax learning combines two opposing optimization problems: one component minimizes an objective while another maximizes it. This paper identifies a failure mode of alternating gradient updates. The solution to the inner maximization can change discontinuously, making it difficult for an alternating method to follow the relevant maximizing solution as the outer variables move.

The proposed K-Beam method addresses this issue by tracking K candidate inner solutions simultaneously. It uses an approximate-subgradient descent algorithm to support the outer optimization. Keeping multiple candidates gives the procedure alternatives when the relevant inner solution changes. The authors report that this can reach solutions missed by previous saddle-point algorithms, with complexity increasing only sublinearly in K.

The paper analyzes conditions under which the algorithm converges to the true solution. Experiments on representative problems, generative adversarial network training, and domain adaptation show substantial improvements in stability and convergence speed. These results support maintaining several competing inner solutions as a practical response to the discontinuities identified in the analysis.
icml-2018-k-beam-minimax-efficient-optim.tldr: K-Beam tracks multiple inner maximizers to address discontinuities that can derail alternating minimax optimization.

paragraphs: A hierarchical reinforcement-learning policy lets higher layers influence lower layers of behavior. This paper builds that hierarchy while training each layer to solve its task directly. A maximum-entropy objective encourages each layer to acquire diverse successful strategies, providing a range of behaviors for the layer above to control.

During training, each layer receives latent random variables sampled from a prior. The maximum-entropy objective leads the policy to use those variables, creating a latent space through which a higher layer can direct lower-level behavior. The mapping from latent variables to actions is constrained to be invertible. Under this construction, the authors state that higher layers retain full expressivity without restricting either level's behavioral possibilities.

Experiments show that adding layers can improve performance over single-layer policies on standard benchmarks. The method also solves more complex sparse-reward tasks by placing higher-level policies over diverse skills learned from simple low-level objectives. The findings support a hierarchy whose usefulness comes from controllable behavioral diversity rather than requiring the lower layers to be unable to solve their own tasks.
icml-2018-latent-space-policies-for-hier.tldr: Maximum-entropy policies create diverse behaviors that higher layers control through latent variables, improving hierarchical learning in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires choosing an output with interconnected parts. MAP perturbation models introduce randomness into maximum-a-posteriori prediction, providing a framework for efficient Gibbs-distribution sampling and predictions robust to random noise. This paper addresses how to learn the parameters of those perturbed predictors with a provable computational guarantee.

The authors develop a randomized learning algorithm that runs in polynomial time. Its objective comes from a new Rademacher-based generalization bound on a perturbed predictor's expected loss. The bound can itself be computed in polynomial time, so it provides a tractable quantity to minimize while explicitly connecting the learning procedure to performance on unseen data.

The paper also derives conditions under which the randomized algorithm guarantees generalization to new examples. Its contribution therefore joins two questions: whether parameter learning is computationally manageable and when the learned predictor is expected to extend beyond its training examples. The generalization result is conditional, while the stated algorithmic contribution is a provably polynomial-time procedure for learning the perturbed model's parameters.
icml-2018-learning-maximum-a-posteriori-.tldr: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm learns perturbed MAP predictors by minimizing a computable generalization bound.

paragraphs: Memory performance can limit computing even when substantial processing capability is available. This paper explores learning the patterns of memory accesses as a step toward better prefetchers: systems intended to anticipate which memory will be needed. The objective is to use deep learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of that anticipation.

The authors connect contemporary prefetching strategies to n-gram models from natural language processing. This frames memory accesses as a sequence-prediction problem and motivates recurrent neural networks as a replacement for the existing prediction mechanism. The connection gives a concrete role to sequence learning within computer hardware architecture rather than treating machine learning as a general-purpose optimization suggestion.

Across a suite of challenging benchmark datasets, neural networks consistently achieve better precision and recall. These findings support their ability to predict memory-access patterns in the evaluated workloads. The authors position the work as an initial step toward practical neural prefetching, so the reported prediction improvements establish potential for that direction rather than a completed demonstration of practical hardware deployment.
icml-2018-learning-memory-access-pattern.tldr: Recurrent neural networks improve memory-access prediction on benchmark datasets, supporting further development of neural memory prefetchers.

paragraphs: This paper studies provably efficient learning of a convolutional network with one hidden layer when input patches may overlap. Its framework covers a general class of patches, including familiar one-dimensional and two-dimensional patch-and-stride arrangements. The guarantees apply under mild conditions on the input distribution.

The proposed Convotron algorithm uses a simple stochastic iterative update inspired by work connecting isotonic regression to neural-network learning. It tolerates noise by requiring the conditional mean of the output to be a one-layer convolutional network; individual observations need not fit that network exactly. Within the stated setting, it converges to the global optimum without special initialization or learning-rate tuning.

The authors also identify a particular simplification for Gaussian inputs. If there is one disjoint patch, while the other patches may be arbitrary, Convotron can efficiently recover the hidden weights by updating only along that patch's direction. Together, these results clarify circumstances in which overlap and noisy observations remain compatible with efficient learning, while keeping the scope to the specified one-layer networks and distributional conditions.
icml-2018-learning-one-convolutional-lay.tldr: Convotron provably learns one-layer convolutional networks with potentially overlapping patches under stated distributional conditions and tolerates noisy observations.

paragraphs: Understanding a multiagent system requires a useful description of how its participants behave. Earlier modeling approaches often depend on task-specific knowledge designed by hand. This paper instead proposes learning representations of agents' policies from a small amount of interaction data, with the aim of providing a general framework for agent modeling.

The learning objective draws on both imitation learning and agent identification. These inspirations connect describing what an agent does with distinguishing its behavior from that of other agents. The resulting algorithm learns policy representations without supervision. Treating behavior as a representation-learning problem makes those learned descriptions available for several subsequent uses rather than tying them to one prediction task.

The authors evaluate the framework in a high-dimensional competitive continuous-control environment and a cooperative communication environment. They demonstrate utility for supervised prediction, unsupervised clustering, and policy optimization with deep reinforcement learning. This variety of uses supports the value of learned policy representations in the tested settings, while the empirical evidence comes from those two types of multiagent environment.
icml-2018-learning-policy-representation.tldr: An unsupervised framework learns policy representations from limited interactions and supports prediction, clustering, and reinforcement learning in multiagent experiments.

paragraphs: Tree-search planners simulate possible futures, evaluate the states they reach, and return information toward the current decision. Monte-Carlo tree search commonly relies on carefully designed rules for these operations. This paper asks whether a neural network can learn where to search, what to evaluate, and how to combine the resulting information.

The proposed MCTSnet embeds simulation-based search within a neural architecture. It expands, evaluates, and backs up vector representations through the search process. All network parameters are trained together using gradient-based optimization. This makes the search procedure itself learnable, including how information from simulated futures contributes to the eventual decision.

The authors evaluate the approach on Sokoban using small searches. In that setting, the learned search algorithm significantly outperforms the MCTS baselines tested. The result demonstrates that learning the internal operations of search can improve planning within a limited-search regime. Its stated empirical scope is small Sokoban searches, where the learned representation and search rules are assessed together as one planning system.
icml-2018-learning-to-search-with-mctsne.tldr: MCTSnets learn the operations of simulation-based tree search and significantly outperform tested MCTS baselines on small Sokoban searches.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a real or complex vector from measurements of its magnitude. The best-known approaches described in this paper proceed iteratively and depend on a good starting estimate. The authors focus on producing that starting point, proposing a class of methods called linear spectral estimators for general nonlinear measurement systems.

Applied to phase retrieval, these estimators provide accurate initialization vectors even when measurements are noisy. They support both structured and random measurement matrices, making the formulation relevant to more than one measurement arrangement. The authors also derive sharp, nonasymptotic bounds on mean-squared error, giving error characterizations that do not rely solely on a limiting regime.

Evaluations cover synthetic and real-world phase retrieval problems. The strongest comparative finding stated is that the proposed estimators significantly outperform existing approaches for structured measurement systems encountered in practice. This matters because an initialization method must work with the measurement structure available in an application. The paper combines that practical performance claim with an analytical account of estimation error.
icml-2018-linear-spectral-estimators-and.tldr: Linear spectral estimators provide accurate phase-retrieval initializations with finite-setting error bounds and strong results for structured measurements.

paragraphs: A predictor can appear reliable at a broad population level while giving less meaningful predictions to smaller subpopulations. This paper introduces multicalibration as a fairness criterion intended to address discrimination introduced during training, including discrimination present in the ground-truth data. The requirement applies calibrated predictions across a specified collection of identifiable subpopulations.

The collection is defined by a class of computations that can identify groups. It can be rich enough to include many overlapping subgroups within a protected group, extending the requirement beyond a single coarse partition. The scope of the guarantee is therefore explicit: it covers every subpopulation identifiable within that chosen computational class.

The authors show that this protection is provably achievable in many settings and can align with accurate prediction. They provide learning algorithms, investigate the computational difficulty of constructing multicalibrated predictors, and establish close connections with agnostic learning. The contribution combines a more detailed group-level reliability target with analysis of when and how a learner can achieve it.
icml-2018-multicalibration-calibration-f.tldr: Multicalibration requires calibrated predictions across computationally identifiable, potentially overlapping subgroups and is provably achievable in many settings.

paragraphs: Controlling a body with nonlinear dynamics requires translating a desired movement into suitable commands. This paper trains a network of spiking neurons with hidden layers to perform that translation for a two-link arm. It uses the supervised FOLLOW scheme to learn an inverse model: given a state trajectory, infer the continuous-time command that produced it.

The network adjusts its connections using a local plasticity rule. Each update involves presynaptic firing and feedback to the postsynaptic neuron about error in the inferred command. This connects the learning signal to information available around an individual connection while supporting learning in a network containing hidden neurons.

The authors introduce a differential feedforward architecture and report lower test error than the other feedforward and recurrent architectures they compare. They also demonstrate using the learned inverse model to make the two-link arm follow a desired trajectory. The findings tie a particular network design and local learning mechanism to successful nonlinear control in the studied arm system.
icml-2018-non-linear-motor-control-by-lo.tldr: A spiking network learns an inverse model through local error-driven updates and uses it to control a two-link arm.

paragraphs: In a partially observable environment, an agent must use its history to interpret what it currently sees. Recurrent Predictive State Policy networks separate this work into a recursive filter and a reactive policy. The filter maintains a belief about the environment, and the policy maps that belief directly to an action.

The filter represents state through predictions of future observations conditioned on past experience and future actions. This predictive state can serve as an equivalent representation of a belief state, allowing the action policy to remain reactive while still permitting optimal behavior. The predictive-state formulation also supplies statistically consistent algorithms for initializing the filter.

Training combines a reward-based policy gradient with gradient descent on prediction error, and the whole architecture remains differentiable. Thus, the state representation is trained both for useful decisions and for predictive accuracy. On the evaluated robotic-control tasks from OpenAI Gym, the authors report strong performance relative to GRUs and finite-memory models, with RPSP networks performing best overall among the compared methods.
icml-2018-recurrent-predictive-state-pol.tldr: RPSP networks combine predictive-state filtering with a reactive policy and achieve the best overall performance among compared models on the evaluated control tasks.

paragraphs: Designing bacterial communities for therapeutic use requires understanding how microbial populations interact and change over time. Learning these dynamics is difficult when abundance measurements are noisy, irregularly spaced, and sparse relative to hundreds of bacterial strains. This paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric dynamical model and an efficient inference algorithm for that setting.

Its central organizing idea is an interaction module: a learned cluster of latent variables with redundant interaction structure. Sharing structure through these modules reduces the expected number of interaction coefficients from O(n²) to O((log n)²). This provides a way to represent complex communities without separately estimating every possible pairwise coefficient.

The Bayesian formulation carries measurement and hidden-state uncertainty through the model. A time-varying auxiliary-variable technique makes inference more efficient by relaxing the hard constraint that population states remain nonnegative. Applications to simulated and real data demonstrate usefulness for identifying dynamics from limited observations and obtaining biological insights relevant to bacteriotherapy design. The contribution addresses model size, uncertainty, and physical constraints within one inference framework.
icml-2018-robust-and-scalable-models-of-.tldr: A Bayesian microbial-dynamics model shares interaction structure across learned modules to support inference from sparse, noisy abundance measurements.

paragraphs: Preconditioning changes how a gradient is transformed into an optimization update, but general preconditioners can require matrices too large to store and manipulate conveniently. Shampoo addresses this cost for parameters organized as tensors. It uses their multidimensional structure to construct a collection of preconditioning matrices instead of one prohibitively large matrix.

Each matrix operates on a single tensor dimension while contracting over the others. This structure-aware design preserves a richer update mechanism while managing the associated computation. The authors establish convergence guarantees for stochastic convex optimization, with an analysis built on matrix trace inequalities. That theoretical scope is distinct from the deep-learning experiments.

In experiments with leading deep-learning models, Shampoo is capable of converging considerably faster than commonly used optimizers. Despite its more elaborate update rule, its measured time per step is comparable to SGD, AdaGrad, and Adam. The reported combination matters practically: a reduction in optimization steps is more useful when the individual steps do not incur a correspondingly large runtime cost.
icml-2018-shampoo-preconditioned-stochas.tldr: Shampoo uses tensor-structured preconditioning to accelerate convergence while keeping per-step runtime comparable to simpler optimizers in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can require many samples and careful hyperparameter choices to train reliably. Soft actor-critic addresses these challenges through an off-policy actor-critic algorithm built around maximum-entropy reinforcement learning. Its actor seeks high expected reward while also retaining as much randomness in its behavior as the objective encourages.

The method combines off-policy updates with a stable stochastic actor-critic formulation. This brings an explicit stochastic actor into a maximum-entropy framework that prior deep methods had formulated through Q-learning. The approach makes behavioral randomness part of the learning objective alongside task success, rather than treating reward as the sole quantity being maximized.

On a range of continuous-control benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, exceeding the prior on-policy and off-policy methods they evaluate. They also find very similar performance across different random seeds, supporting the claim of stable learning in those experiments. The findings connect competitive control performance with reproducibility across training runs, addressing both effectiveness and the brittleness motivating the method.
icml-2018-soft-actor-critic-off-policy-m.tldr: Soft actor-critic combines off-policy learning with a maximum-entropy stochastic actor to deliver strong, stable continuous-control benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent is an approximate-inference method for complex probability distributions, but its standard form needs gradients of the target density. That requirement prevents its direct use when those gradients are unavailable. This paper introduces GF-SVGD, a variant that replaces the unavailable target gradient with a surrogate.

Using a surrogate can introduce bias, so the method reweights the gradients in a form designed to correct it. The authors show that the resulting algorithm can be interpreted as ordinary SVGD with a particular kernel choice. This relationship is central to their analysis: GF-SVGD directly inherits SVGD's theoretical properties through that interpretation.

The paper also discusses empirical choices of surrogate gradient and proposes an annealed version of GF-SVGD. In the reported empirical studies, the annealed method consistently outperforms several recent gradient-free MCMC methods. The contribution therefore includes both a principled way to replace target gradients and an experimentally successful inference variant, with the comparative performance claim grounded in the studies conducted.
icml-2018-stein-variational-gradient-des.tldr: GF-SVGD substitutes reweighted surrogate gradients for unavailable target gradients while retaining a theoretical connection to standard SVGD.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks are attractive for their ability to express calibrated uncertainty, but deciding how large a network should be remains a model-selection problem. This paper focuses on compactness, including the question of how many nodes are needed. The goal is to reduce unnecessary model capacity while preserving useful predictive performance.

The starting point is earlier work placing a horseshoe prior over node pre-activations. That prior can effectively deactivate nodes that do not contribute to explaining the data. It therefore provides a mechanism for choosing an effective network size within learning, with the data helping determine which nodes remain useful.

The authors propose several advances in modeling and inference within this approach. They report that these changes consistently produce more compact learned models while maintaining prediction quality, especially when samples are limited, including reinforcement-learning settings. The stated result links network-size reduction with preserved performance: the value comes from removing unhelpful nodes without paying a corresponding predictive cost in the settings considered.
icml-2018-structured-variational-learnin.tldr: Modeling and inference advances for horseshoe-prior Bayesian networks improve compactness while maintaining predictive performance, especially with limited samples.

paragraphs: Longitudinal event records contain many event types whose occurrences may be related over time. Temporal Poisson square root graphical models extend an existing graphical-model family to represent these relationships. By considering every pair of event types, they offer a broad view of whether one type's occurrence could encourage or inhibit another.

The method learns a collection of linked Poisson square root models that share a common parameter template. Joint estimation uses a Poisson pseudo-likelihood approximation to avoid the more expensive original pseudo-likelihood computation. Under mild assumptions, the authors prove sparsistency: the approximation can recover the underlying pattern of present and absent relationships in the model.

The empirical application uses a large electronic health record containing millions of prescription and diagnosis events to detect adverse drug reaction signals. The learned models recover these signals effectively and efficiently in the reported experiments. This connects the computational approximation to a substantial event-data application, while the recovered signals provide evidence for detection rather than a claim that every modeled relationship establishes a causal drug effect.
icml-2018-temporal-poisson-square-root-g.tldr: Temporal Poisson square root models efficiently estimate event relationships and recover adverse drug reaction signals from large electronic health records.

paragraphs: An agent can earn high rewards while leaving its strategy difficult to understand. This paper examines that problem through deep reinforcement-learning agents in Atari environments. It focuses on saliency maps as a way to reveal which parts of the visual input matter to an agent's decisions and how that pattern changes during learning.

The authors introduce a method for generating useful maps and apply it to three questions: what strong agents attend to, whether their decisions rest on appropriate reasons, and how their behavior develops through training. These uses connect visualization to concrete questions about policy execution and learning, giving observers a way to inspect behavior beyond the final reward score.

The paper also tests the method with non-expert human participants. Access to its saliency information improves their ability to reason about the agents. Together, the case studies and human evaluation show that the visualizations can provide substantial insight into decisions and learning behavior in the studied Atari settings, making the agents' strategies more accessible to human interpretation.
icml-2018-visualizing-and-understanding-.tldr: Saliency maps reveal aspects of Atari agents' decisions and learning, improving non-experts' ability to reason about their behavior.
